title: Publish a status page & SLA
summary: Give customers a public uptime commitment: stand up the status page on your domain, wire the uptime monitors, draft the SLA with its credit terms, get counsel over the credits, and put the SLA into contracts and the site.

parts.title: Choose a status-page provider
parts.guidance: Compare status-page services using the components customers need to see, the people who will publish incidents and the notification paths subscribers will use. Try a draft incident, update and recovery before choosing. Check custom-domain behavior, access controls and the quoted plan cost. Purchase within the operations owner's budget authority, and ensure responders have a way to reach the page and communicate if the main application or usual sign-in path is unavailable.

parts.title: Create components and wire uptime monitors
parts.guidance: Name components in terms customers recognize, then map monitors to the user journeys each component represents. Decide when a failed check should page a responder and when it should change public status; those need not be the same action. Activate monitoring and public updates within the service owner's authorized scope. Use a controlled failure and recovery to verify the component, responder and public message, and identify outages the checks would miss.

parts.title: Publish the page on your domain
parts.guidance: Connect the status hostname using the provider's DNS instructions and the domain owner's change authority. Publish the communications owner's cleared components and content, then verify HTTPS and the live page from an external connection. Use a controlled drill or client-side simulation to test access without depending on the main application; do not take production down for this check. Test a notification with a designated recipient and make the fallback communication route available to responders.

references.title: Set up a primary DNS zone

parts.title: Draft the SLA (uptime target, credits)
parts.guidance: Draft the SLA from the service measurements and customer commitments the company can actually support. Define the covered service, measurement window, outage calculation, exclusions, claim process and proposed remedy. Work through an outage example with engineering and finance, including what data establishes the event and how the credit would be calculated. Mark commercial choices and unresolved terms for counsel, keeping the internal reliability target distinct from the promise proposed for the contract.

parts.title: Counsel reviews the SLA credit terms
parts.guidance: Give counsel the SLA draft, service agreement and worked outage examples. Resolve inconsistent definitions, exclusions, claim procedures and remedy language across the documents. Engineering should confirm that the calculation can be reproduced from available measurements; finance should confirm it can administer the remedy. Record the legal revisions and commercial decisions against the specific version cleared for customer use.

parts.title: Add the SLA to contracts and the site
parts.guidance: Publish the version cleared by the legal and commercial owners in the intended contract templates and public pages. Check document references, download links and version identifiers. Have the legal owner determine how existing customers are affected before changing their terms; a website edit alone does not implement that process. Give sales and support the applicable version and claim instructions, and verify that the live materials agree.

metadata.supportReason: Status pages, monitors, and DNS are fully API-driven; the SLA’s credit terms need counsel before they go into contracts.
